## Proof

Let \(X\) be an uncountable well-ordered set, and for \(x\in X\) let \(I(x)=\{y\in X:y<x\}\).

Define
\[
B=\{x\in X : I(x)\text{ is finite}\}.
\]

**Claim 1.** \(B\) is a (proper) initial segment of \(X\).

*Downward closed.* If \(x\in B\) and \(y<x\), then \(I(y)\subseteq I(x)\), so \(I(y)\) is finite, hence \(y\in B\).

*Closed under successor.* If \(x\in B\) and \(s(x)\) is the immediate successor of \(x\), then \(I(s(x))=I(x)\cup\{x\}\), which is finite, so \(s(x)\in B\).

*Proper.* Suppose \(B=X\). Then every initial segment \(I(x)\) is finite. A well-ordered set in which every proper initial segment is finite has order type at most \(\omega\) (the only ordinals all of whose initial segments are finite are the finite ordinals and \(\omega\)). Hence \(|X|\le\aleph_0\), contradicting the uncountability of \(X\). So \(B\neq X\).

Since \(B\) is a proper initial segment, \(B=I(c)\) where \(c=\min(X\setminus B)\).

**Claim 2.** \(B\) is infinite.

If \(B\) were finite, then \(I(c)=B\) would be finite, forcing \(c\in B\), contradicting \(c\notin B\). Hence \(B\) is infinite.

**Claim 3.** \(B\) has order type \(\omega\), so \(I(c)\) is countably infinite.

\(B\) is an infinite well-ordered set in which every element has a finite initial segment (by definition of \(B\)). The only infinite well-order with all proper initial segments finite is \(\omega\). Therefore \(B\cong\omega\), i.e. \(I(c)\) is countably infinite.

Thus \(c\in X\) satisfies \(I(c)\) countably infinite. \(\square\)
